title: Glucose plus fructose: beating the absorption limit
goal: Explain why glucose alone caps out near 60 g·h⁻¹, how adding fructose raises the cap, which ratio to use, and what is still unknown about 120 g·h⁻¹.

steps.title: The glucose bottleneck
steps.text:
Swallowed glucose, and [maltodextrin](g:maltodextrin) (which the gut cuts back to glucose), crosses the gut wall through one transporter, [SGLT1](g:sglt1), and SGLT1 is saturated at around 60 g·h⁻¹ [[c:tr-sglt1]]. Measured with labelled glucose, the [exogenous oxidation rate](g:exogenous-oxidation-rate) of glucose alone tops out near 1 g·min⁻¹ (60 g·h⁻¹), however much more you swallow [[c:tr-limit-oxidation]].

So the bottleneck is absorption in the gut, not the muscle. Take 90 g·h⁻¹ of glucose alone and the extra 30 g·h⁻¹ isn't burned during the effort: it builds up in the intestine, a recipe for gut trouble.

claims.text: Glucose is absorbed through SGLT1, which is thought to saturate at an intake of around 60 g·h⁻¹.

evidence.quote: It is believed that glucose uses the sodium-dependent transporter (SGLT1) for absorption, which becomes saturated at a carbohydrate intake of around 60 g/h.
It is believed that at this ingestion rate, the sodium-glucose linked transporters (SGLT1) in the small intestine become saturated

claims.text: A single carbohydrate source can be oxidised at up to about 60 g·h⁻¹; the limit lies in absorption, and higher intakes need multiple transportable carbohydrates to avoid carbohydrate accumulating in the intestine.

evidence.quote: A single carbohydrate source can be oxidized at rates up to approximately 60 g/h and this is the recommendation for exercise that is more prolonged (2-3 h).
It was found that limitations to carbohydrate oxidation were in the absorptive process most likely because of a saturation of carbohydrate transporters.
Carbohydrate ingested at such high ingestion rates must be a multiple transportable carbohydrates to allow high oxidation rates and prevent the accumulation of carbohydrate in the intestine.

steps.title: A second door: fructose
steps.text:
Fructose enters through a different transporter, [GLUT5](g:glut5), so it doesn't queue behind glucose. In a landmark study, cyclists drank 1.2 g·min⁻¹ of glucose plus 0.6 g·min⁻¹ of fructose: peak exogenous oxidation reached 1.26 g·min⁻¹, against 0.80 g·min⁻¹ with glucose alone [[c:tr-jentjens]]. Later studies pushed it to about 1.75 g·min⁻¹ [[c:tr-mtc-max]].

This is the idea behind [multiple transportable carbohydrates](g:multiple-transportable-carbohydrates): open two doors and more carbohydrate gets in per hour. It's why the target of up to 90 g·h⁻¹ for long events assumes glucose plus fructose.

claims.text: Glucose plus fructose ingested at high rates gave peak exogenous oxidation about 55% higher than glucose alone (1.26 vs 0.80 g·min⁻¹).

evidence.quote: Peak exogenous carbohydrate oxidation rates were approximately 55% higher (P < 0.001) in Fruc+Glu (1.26 +/- 0.07 g/min) compared with Med-Glu and High-Glu (0.80 +/- 0.04 and 0.83 +/- 0.05 g/min, respectively).

claims.text: With multiple transportable carbohydrates, exogenous oxidation can reach about 1.75 g·min⁻¹, well above the old 1 g·min⁻¹ ceiling.

evidence.quote: Exogenous carbohydrate oxidation rates reach values of 1.75 g/min whereas previously it was thought that 1 g/min was the absolute maximum.

steps.title: From g·min⁻¹ to g·h⁻¹
steps.problem: Oxidation studies report g·min⁻¹; race plans use g·h⁻¹. Convert 1.26 g·min⁻¹ (glucose + fructose) and 0.80 g·min⁻¹ (glucose alone), and find the gain.
steps: An hour has 60 minutes, so multiply by 60.
Gain = 75.6 − 48 ≈ 28 g·h⁻¹ more carbohydrate burned from what was swallowed, every hour.

steps.title: Does it make you faster?
steps.text:
Burning more only matters if you race faster. In one study, eight male cyclists rode 2 h, then a time trial of about 1 h, drinking 1.8 g·min⁻¹ of glucose alone or of glucose plus fructose. The blend made them 8% faster [[c:tr-currell]]. A review of 14 studies found 1–9% more power over 2.5–3 h with the blends, in men and mostly in cycling [[c:tr-rowlands]].

The benefits show mainly in efforts of 2.5 h or more, from the third hour on. In shorter races the blend is no better than glucose alone, though no worse either [[c:tr-when]].

claims.text: A glucose + fructose drink improved cycling time-trial performance by 8% compared with glucose alone at the same intake.

evidence.quote: Ingestion of GF led to an 8% improvement in cycling time-trial performance compared with ingestion of G.

claims.text: Across 14 studies of 2.5–3 h exercise in men, fructose–glucose blends improved mean power by about 1–9% over glucose or maltodextrin alone.

evidence.quote: Overall, 14 studies contained estimates of 2.5-3.0-h endurance performance in men, mostly in cycling.

Relative to isocaloric glucose/maltodextrin, the ingestion of 0.5-1.0:1-ratio fructose:glucose/maltodextrin beverages at 1.3-2.4 g carbohydrate·min(-1) produced small to moderate enhancements (1-9 %; 95 % confidence interval 0-19) in mean power.

claims.text: Performance benefits of multiple transportable carbohydrates appear mainly in exercise of 2.5 h or more; in shorter efforts they are at least as good as other carbohydrate.

evidence.quote: Performance benefits have generally been observed in studies that are 2.5 h or longer and effects start to become visible in the third hour of exercise

When exercise duration is shorter, multiple transportable carbohydrates may not have the same performance benefits [ 38 ], but it must be noted that the effects are at least similar to other carbohydrate sources.

steps.title: 2:1 or 1:0.8?
steps.text:
Ratios are written glucose : fructose, with maltodextrin counted as glucose. The classic blend is 2:1: glucose at about the SGLT1 limit plus half as much fructose. It became the standard advice [[c:tr-ratio-classic]].

Newer work favours a ratio nearer 1:0.8. Cyclists drinking 1.8 g·min⁻¹ burned about 11% more of a 1:0.8 blend than of a 2:1 blend, and reported the least stomach fullness, cramping and nausea with it [[c:tr-ratio-08]].

The case for 1:0.8 rests on a handful of small studies, mostly of male cyclists, so treat it as a good bet rather than settled.

claims.text: Most studies of glucose + fructose used a 2:1 ratio, which became the standard recommendation.

evidence.quote: Most studies investigating combined ingestion of glucose-based carbohydrates and fructose utilized a 2:1 glucose:fructose ratio, and this has since become a standard recommendation

claims.text: A ratio near 1:0.8 glucose:fructose gives higher oxidation efficiency and better gut comfort than 2:1.

evidence.quote: Mean exogenous carbohydrate oxidation rates were 1.04, 1.14, and 1.05 g/min (coefficient of variation 20%) in 0.5-, 0.8-, and 1.25-Ratios, respectively
Increases in stomach fullness, abdominal cramping, and nausea were lowest with the 0.8- followed by the 1.25-Ratio solution.
when ingested at 1.5-1.8 g·min(-1), a 0.8:1 fructose:glucose ratio conveyed the highest exogenous carbohydrate energy and endurance power compared with lower or higher fructose:glucose ratios.

However, a closer examination of the literature reveals that a ratio closer to unity (i.e., 1:0.8 glucose:fructose) is superior both from the perspective of oxidation efficiency (i.e., the fraction of ingested carbohydrates being oxidized) as well as gut comfort

steps.title: Splitting an hourly target by ratio
steps.problem: A rider wants 90 g·h⁻¹. How much glucose and fructose is that in a 2:1 blend, and in a 1:0.8 blend?
steps: Add the parts of the ratio: 2:1 has 2 + 1 = 3 parts; 1:0.8 has 1 + 0.8 = 1.8 parts.
2:1: one part = 90 ÷ 3 = 30 g, so 60 g glucose + 30 g fructose.
1:0.8: one part = 90 ÷ 1.8 = 50 g, so 50 g glucose + 0.8 × 50 = 40 g fructose.
Check: each pair adds back to 90 g. The 1:0.8 blend puts less glucose through SGLT1 (50 g, below its limit) and more through GLUT5.

steps.title: The 120 g·h⁻¹ debate
steps.text:
Some professional cyclists and triathletes now take 100–120 g·h⁻¹. In 11 highly trained male cyclists riding 3 h, 120 g·h⁻¹ (1:0.8) raised exogenous oxidation over the last hour to 1.51 g·min⁻¹, against 1.29 g·min⁻¹ with 90 g·h⁻¹ (2:1). But the body's own carbohydrate use was no lower, dose and ratio changed together, and performance wasn't measured [[c:tr-120-podlogar]].

The [oxidation efficiency](g:oxidation-efficiency) also fell: a bigger share of what was swallowed was still unburned during the ride. In one trial of elite mountain runners, 120 g·h⁻¹ gave lower blood markers of muscle damage than 90 g·h⁻¹ [[c:tr-120-viribay]]. Whether 120 makes you faster is still open.

claims.text: 120 g·h⁻¹ (1:0.8) raised exogenous oxidation compared with 90 g·h⁻¹ (2:1) but did not reduce use of the body's own carbohydrate; performance remains to be tested.

evidence.quote: However, higher exogenous CHO oxidation rates did not translate into sparing of endogenous CHO utilisation.
Further studies should investigate potential performance effects of such carbohydrate ingestion strategies.

claims.text: In elite male mountain runners, 120 g·h⁻¹ during a mountain marathon gave lower muscle-damage markers the next day than 60 or 90 g·h⁻¹.

evidence.quote: Conclusion: High CHO intake (120 g/h) during a mountain marathon could limit the EIMD observed by CK, LDH and GOT and internal exercise load compared to CHO ingestion of 60 and 90 g/h.

debate.question: Is 120 g·h⁻¹ better than 90 g·h⁻¹ for long races?

sides.position: Possibly: 120 g·h⁻¹ raises exogenous oxidation, is tolerated by trained athletes as drink, gel or chews, and in one trial lowered muscle-damage markers.
Not shown: it didn't spare the body's own carbohydrate, dose–response studies find performance gains flattening near 80–90 g·h⁻¹, and no well-controlled trial shows faster racing.

steps.title: How much of what you swallow gets burned?
steps.problem: At 90 g·h⁻¹, riders burned swallowed carbohydrate at 1.29 g·min⁻¹. What was the oxidation efficiency?
steps: Put both rates in the same units: 1.29 g·min⁻¹ × 60 = 77.4 g·h⁻¹.
The other 14% (about 13 g·h⁻¹) was still in the gut, stored, or burned later.

points: Glucose and maltodextrin share one gut transporter, SGLT1, which saturates near 60 g·h⁻¹; glucose alone is burned at no more than about 1 g·min⁻¹.
Fructose enters through GLUT5, so glucose + fructose raises exogenous oxidation to about 1.3–1.75 g·min⁻¹.
Blends improve performance by about 1–9% in efforts of 2.5 h or more; in shorter races they are no better than glucose.
2:1 is the classic ratio; 1:0.8 looks a little better for oxidation and gut comfort, from a few small studies.
120 g·h⁻¹ raises exogenous oxidation but doesn't spare the body's own carbohydrate; a performance benefit over 90 g·h⁻¹ is unproven.

variants.stem: At most, about how fast can the body burn swallowed glucose when glucose is the only carbohydrate taken?

options.why: Right: glucose alone tops out near 1 g·min⁻¹ because its gut transporter saturates.
Rates like that need fructose as well, through a second transporter.
30 g·h⁻¹ is the low end of the advice for 1–2.5 h, not the ceiling.

options.text: No ceiling: it rises with intake
options.why: Oxidation plateaus: swallowing more than about 60 g·h⁻¹ of glucose doesn't raise it.

variants.stem: Why does oxidation of swallowed glucose level off near 1 g·min⁻¹ even when athletes take more?

options.text: Its gut transporter, SGLT1, is saturated
options.why: Right: the limit is absorption from the intestine, not what the muscles can burn.

options.text: Muscle can't burn more than 1 g·min⁻¹ of carbohydrate
options.why: In hard exercise the body burns 2–3 g·min⁻¹ of carbohydrate or more, mostly from glycogen; the cap is on what the gut absorbs.

options.text: The liver stores all glucose above that rate
options.why: The extra glucose mostly never gets past the gut wall in the first place.

options.text: Insulin blocks glucose uptake during exercise
options.why: Contraction moves GLUT4 to the muscle membrane during exercise; uptake into muscle isn't the block.

variants.stem: A runner takes 100 g·h⁻¹ from glucose-only gels in a marathon and is bloated with diarrhoea by 90 min. Best explanation?

options.text: Glucose beyond the SGLT1 limit builds up in his gut
options.why: Right: about 40 g·h⁻¹ more than SGLT1 can absorb stays in the intestine.

options.text: His muscles are burning too much carbohydrate
options.why: Burning carbohydrate doesn't upset the gut; unabsorbed carbohydrate does.

options.text: The gels contain too little sodium
options.why: Sodium matters for fluid balance, but it doesn't explain carbohydrate piling up in the gut.

options.text: Glucose gels raise blood glucose too high
options.why: During hard running, blood glucose is used fast; the problem is in the gut, before absorption.

variants.stem: Why does adding fructose to glucose raise how much swallowed carbohydrate you can burn per hour?

options.text: Fructose enters through a different transporter, GLUT5
options.why: Right: with a second door open, more carbohydrate is absorbed per hour.

options.text: Fructose makes SGLT1 carry glucose faster
options.why: Fructose doesn't speed up SGLT1; it bypasses it.

options.text: Fructose holds much more energy per gram
options.why: Fructose and glucose have about the same energy per gram; the gain is in absorption.

options.text: Fructose stops the liver from releasing glucose
options.why: That wouldn't raise exogenous oxidation; the gain comes from absorbing more.

variants.stem: In a study, glucose plus fructose was oxidised at 1.3 g·min⁻¹. What is that in g·h⁻¹?

options.why: That multiplies by 100, not by the 60 minutes in an hour.
That is 60 ÷ 1.3: divided instead of multiplied.
That multiplies by 6, not 60.

variants.stem: A trained cyclist burns swallowed carbohydrate at 1.5 g·min⁻¹. What is that in g·h⁻¹?

options.why: That multiplies by 100, not by 60.
That is 60 ÷ 1.5: divided instead of multiplied.
That multiplies by 6, not 60.

variants.stem: Glucose alone was oxidised at 0.8 g·min⁻¹. What is that in g·h⁻¹?

options.why: That multiplies by 100, not by 60.
That is 60 ÷ 0.8: divided instead of multiplied.
That multiplies by 6, not 60.

variants.stem: Who is most likely to race faster by switching from a glucose-only drink to glucose plus fructose at the same high intake?

options.text: A triathlete on a 5 h Ironman bike leg
options.why: Right: blends help mainly beyond 2.5 h, when absorption above the glucose limit pays off.

options.text: A cyclist in a 50 min criterium
options.why: In efforts of about 1 h, a blend is no better than glucose; small amounts or a rinse do the job.

options.text: A runner in a 10 km race
options.why: A 10 km race is too short for the absorption limit to matter.

options.text: A cyclist doing a 4 km pursuit
options.why: A few minutes of racing doesn't depend on carbohydrate swallowed during it.

variants.stem: A triathlete wants 72 g·h⁻¹ in a 1:0.8 glucose:fructose ratio. How much glucose and fructose per hour?

options.why: Right: 72 ÷ 1.8 = 40 g per part; fructose = 0.8 × 40 = 32 g.
That is the 2:1 split (72 ÷ 3 = 24 g per part).
That treats 0.8 as the glucose share (72 × 0.8 ≈ 58 g); the ratio means 1 part glucose to 0.8 parts fructose.
That is a 1:1 split; 1:0.8 has a little less fructose than glucose.

variants.solution: Parts = 1 + 0.8 = 1.8. One part = 72 ÷ 1.8 = 40 g. Glucose = 40 g; fructose = 0.8 × 40 = 32 g. Check: 40 + 32 = 72 g.

variants.stem: A drink mix supplies 75 g·h⁻¹ in a 2:1 glucose:fructose ratio. How much glucose and fructose per hour?

options.why: Right: 75 ÷ 3 = 25 g per part; glucose = 2 × 25 = 50 g.
That is roughly the 1:0.8 split, not 2:1.
That is a 1:1 split.
That splits 75 into 4 parts (a 3:1 ratio); 2:1 has 3 parts.

variants.solution: Parts = 2 + 1 = 3. One part = 75 ÷ 3 = 25 g. Glucose = 2 × 25 = 50 g; fructose = 25 g.

variants.stem: A pro cyclist takes 108 g·h⁻¹ in a 1:0.8 glucose:fructose ratio. How much glucose and fructose per hour?

options.why: Right: 108 ÷ 1.8 = 60 g per part; fructose = 0.8 × 60 = 48 g.
That is the 2:1 split (108 ÷ 3 = 36 g per part).
That treats 0.8 as the glucose share (108 × 0.8 ≈ 86 g).
That is a 1:1 split.

variants.solution: Parts = 1.8. One part = 108 ÷ 1.8 = 60 g. Glucose = 60 g, at about the SGLT1 limit; fructose = 0.8 × 60 = 48 g.

variants.stem: A rider wants about 100 g·h⁻¹ in a 5 h gran fondo but gets bloated on 2:1 drinks. What does the evidence suggest she try?

options.text: A blend nearer 1:0.8, practised in training first
options.why: Right: small studies find 1:0.8 burned a little better with less fullness and nausea; worth testing in long rides.

options.text: Glucose only, to keep things simple
options.why: Glucose alone saturates near 60 g·h⁻¹; at 100 g·h⁻¹ even more would sit in her gut.

options.text: Fructose only, since it uses its own transporter
options.why: GLUT5 alone carries even less than SGLT1; fructose works as an addition, not a replacement.

options.text: Stay on 2:1, as the ratio can't affect the gut
options.why: In one trial, stomach fullness, cramping and nausea were lowest with the 0.8 ratio.

variants.stem: Riders swallowed 120 g·h⁻¹ and burned it at 1.51 g·min⁻¹ over the last hour. What was the oxidation efficiency?

options.why: That is 1.51 ÷ 120: g·min⁻¹ was divided by g·h⁻¹ without converting.
That is 120 ÷ 90.6, upside down; efficiency can't exceed 100%.
That reads 90.6 g·h⁻¹ as a percentage without dividing by the 120 g·h⁻¹ swallowed.

variants.solution: Burned = 1.51 g·min⁻¹ × 60 = 90.6 g·h⁻¹. Efficiency = 90.6 ÷ 120 = 0.755 ≈ 76%. At 90 g·h⁻¹ it was about 86%: more in, but a smaller share burned.

variants.stem: In a trial, riders swallowed 75 g·h⁻¹ and burned it at 1.0 g·min⁻¹. What was the oxidation efficiency?

options.why: That is 1.0 ÷ 75: g·min⁻¹ was divided by g·h⁻¹ without converting.
That is 75 ÷ 60, upside down; efficiency can't exceed 100%.
That reads 60 g·h⁻¹ as a percentage without dividing by the 75 g·h⁻¹ swallowed.

variants.stem: A coach says 120 g·h⁻¹ is now proven better than 90 g·h⁻¹ for long races. What is the fairest summary?

options.text: It raises exogenous oxidation, but faster racing isn't shown
options.why: Right: more swallowed carbohydrate is burned, but the body's own use isn't spared and performance hasn't been tested well.

options.text: Proven, as it spares muscle and liver glycogen
options.why: The 120 vs 90 g·h⁻¹ study found no sparing of the body's own carbohydrate.

options.text: Disproven, as nobody can burn over 90 g·h⁻¹
options.why: At 120 g·h⁻¹, riders burned about 1.5 g·min⁻¹ (90 g·h⁻¹), and some reached 2.0 g·min⁻¹.

options.text: Proven, since top professionals use it
options.why: What pros do isn't evidence that it works; it is a reason to test it.

variants.stem: The 120 vs 90 g·h⁻¹ study tested 11 highly trained men, measured fuel use (not race times), and was part-funded by a training-software company. Which claim goes beyond what it can show?

options.text: Amateur women will race faster on 120 g·h⁻¹
options.why: Right: performance wasn't measured, and the sample was highly trained men; this claim goes past the data on both counts.

options.text: 120 g·h⁻¹ raised exogenous oxidation in these riders
options.why: That is what the study measured and found.

options.text: Use of their own carbohydrate didn't differ between doses
options.why: That was also measured: endogenous oxidation was about the same.

options.text: At 90 g·h⁻¹, exogenous oxidation was about 1.3 g·min⁻¹
options.why: That is a measured result (1.29 g·min⁻¹), not an extrapolation.
